references.text: God does not take pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that he turns from his ways. [ref:Ezek 18:23|Ezekiel 18:23] expresses God's heart for repentance – the same joy over one sinner who repents as Jesus describes in Luke 15:7.
[ref:Ezek 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11] emphasizes that God does not delight in the death of the wicked, but desires that he turn and live. This shows the same divine joy over repentance.

[ref:Luke 15:10|Luke 15:10] repeats the same point in the parable of the lost coin: there is joy among God's angels over one sinner who repents. The parallel confirms the theme of heavenly joy over repentance.

In the parable of the prodigal son, the same joy is expressed when the father says: "this son of mine was dead and is alive again" ([ref:Luke 15:24|Luke 15:24]). All three parables in Luke 15 are about the joy over what was lost and found.

[ref:Luke 5:32|Luke 5:32] – Jesus says that he has not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. This supports the contrast between the ninety-nine righteous and the one sinner who repents.

[ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9] says that the Lord does not wish for anyone to perish, but that all should come to repentance. This confirms God's desire and joy over repentance, in line with Jesus' words in Luke 15:7.

[ref:Acts 11:18|Acts 11:18] – The church praises God because he has also given the Gentiles repentance leading to life. The spontaneous joy over repentance reflects the joy in heaven that Jesus speaks of.

[ref:Luke 15:4-6|Luke 15:4-6] is the parable of the lost sheep itself, which forms the basis for the statement in verse 7. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to search for the one and rejoices when he finds it.

[ref:Isa 55:7|Isaiah 55:7] calls on the wicked to forsake their way and turn to the Lord, who will have mercy on him. God's mercy toward those who repent is closely connected with the heavenly joy over repentance.
[ref:Matt 18:13|Matthew 18:13] is Matthew's parallel to the parable of the lost sheep, where the shepherd rejoices more over the one that was found than over the ninety-nine who did not go astray.

[ref:Luke 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2] provides the context for Jesus' parable: tax collectors and sinners came to hear him, while the Pharisees and scribes murmured. Jesus' words about joy in heaven are a response to this murmuring.
